Report_ID: Participants experiencing at least one symptomatic, culture-positive urinary tract infection during treatment
Title: A randomized trial to evaluate effectiveness and cost effectiveness of naturopathic cranberry products as prophylaxis against urinary tract infection in women
Author: Lynn Stothers
Comment: The two eligible cranberry arms were combined as required by the synthesis plan by summing the explicitly reported arm counts: juice 10/50 plus tablet 9/50 = 19/100. The control is 16/50. The paper reports 50 randomized per arm and presents outcome percentages using those denominators, but it does not explicitly identify the analysis as intention-to-treat or provide a distinct final analysed sample. Therefore randomized denominators were used. The reported p<0.05 values apply separately to juice versus placebo and tablet versus placebo, not to the combined cranberry comparison, so no p value was entered. No RR or confidence interval was reported by the paper.
domain: Urology; prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection
Medium: Oral cranberry juice or concentrated cranberry tablets
Participant type: Sexually active adult women with recurrent symptomatic, culture-positive UTIs
Outcome measurement: At least one symptomatic UTI during treatment; the paper defined culture positivity as at least 100,000 single organisms per millilitre
Outcome variable: Participants experiencing at least one symptomatic, culture-positive urinary tract infection during treatment
outcome_family: occurrence of symptomatic, culture-verified urinary tract infection

Title: Consumption of a cranberry juice beverage lowered the number of clinical urinary tract infection episodes in women with a recent history of urinary tract infection
Author: Maki et al.
Comment: The analysis used the intent-to-treat population (all 373 randomized participants), with observation time censored when study product was discontinued. The paper does not report participant-level culture-positive event counts by arm. The 30 cranberry and 34 placebo microbiologically positive clinical UTIs reported later are episode counts, not numbers of participants, and were therefore not entered as events. Comment: Used the reported analysed samples for the cranberry and control arms (50 in each); the paper does not explicitly call this an intention-to-treat analysis. Title: Cranberry Juice Fails to Prevent Recurrent Urinary Tract Infection: Results From a Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial
Author: Cibele Barbosa-Cesnik et al.
Comment: Used the explicitly reported intention-to-treat randomized denominators (155 cranberry, 164 placebo). Although the Results calls the 54 recurrences 'episodes,' participants were followed until a confirmed UTI or 6 months, so 31 and 23 represent participants experiencing the first recurrence and are usable as participant-level events. The reported cumulative incidences (19.3% and 14.6%) are Kaplan–Meier estimates and were not substituted for raw event counts. The paper did not report a risk ratio; the unadjusted hazard ratio is recorded only because it was explicitly reported. P=.21 is from the log-rank comparison.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('8 oz of 27% low-calorie cranberry juice cocktail twice daily') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
